set1.q: A 50-year-old woman with symptomatic varicose veins has worn stockings and exercised faithfully for several months with persistent aching. Duplex ultrasound confirms great saphenous vein reflux. Which is the most appropriate next treatment?
opts: Surgical valvuloplasty
Valvuloplasty is a surgical option for chronic venous insufficiency and carries a high risk of postoperative clot. Varicose veins with reflux are treated with ablation.
Venous ablation therapy
Correct. Stockings are tried for weeks to months before venous ablation is offered, and the goal is to improve symptoms and appearance. She has now failed that trial, with reflux confirmed.
Lifelong observation only
Observation is reasonable for mild disease, but she has persistent symptoms after a full conservative trial. Ablation is offered once stockings fail.
Oral flavonoid therapy
Flavonoids are used to increase venous tone, but at most they are an add-on and leave the reflux untreated. Persistent symptoms with confirmed reflux call for venous ablation.

opts: Above 3
The overlap ends once the international normalized ratio is above 2, the therapeutic threshold for this indication. Waiting for a value above 3 would prolong the injections without benefit.
Above 4
An international normalized ratio above 4 is over-anticoagulated and raises the bleeding risk. The heparin overlap stops once warfarin is therapeutic, at a value above 2.
Above 2

Correct. Parenteral therapy overlaps with warfarin for at least five days and until the international normalized ratio is above 2, when warfarin has reached its therapeutic effect and the heparin can stop.
Above 1
An international normalized ratio just above 1 is barely different from normal, so warfarin has not yet taken effect. The overlap continues until the value is above 2.

set1.q: A 45-year-old woman has a catheter-related deep vein thrombosis of the right arm and asks how likely a pulmonary embolism is compared with a leg clot. Which statement is accurate?
opts: Up to 6%, versus 15 to 30% for leg clots
Correct. Pulmonary embolism occurs in up to 6% of upper-extremity deep vein thromboses, versus 15% to 30% of lower-extremity clots. Arm clots are only 5% to 10% of all deep vein thromboses.
15 to 30%, versus up to 6% for leg clots
This reverses the figures. Pulmonary embolism complicates 15% to 30% of lower-extremity clots and only up to 6% of upper-extremity clots, so her risk is the lower one.
About 3% for arm and leg clots alike

About 3% is the estimated fatal-embolism rate for untreated symptomatic non-massive pulmonary embolism, not the frequency of embolism, which differs by site: up to 6% for arm and 15% to 30% for leg clots.
Under 1% for arm clots, 6% for leg clots
Under 1% is the untreated fatal-embolism estimate for a clot without pulmonary embolism. The actual frequency of embolism is up to 6% for arm clots and 15% to 30% for leg clots.

set1.q: A 68-year-old woman with active pancreatic cancer, which supplies the hypercoagulable component of the Virchow triad, has an acute proximal deep vein thrombosis of the left leg. She also has active gastrointestinal bleeding. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Systemic thrombolysis

Thrombolysis breaks down clots and carries a high bleeding risk, so it is dangerous with active hemorrhage. It is reserved for large proximal clots or stable pulmonary embolism in patients who can bleed safely.
Outpatient rivaroxaban
Rivaroxaban is a direct factor Xa inhibitor, an anticoagulant, and active bleeding contraindicates anticoagulants. Her bleeding must be controlled first, and a filter covers the clot risk meanwhile.
Inferior vena cava filter

Correct. An inferior vena cava filter is used for acute proximal lower-extremity deep vein thrombosis when there is active bleeding or anticoagulation is otherwise contraindicated. The filter keeps the clot from traveling to the lungs and causing pulmonary embolism.
Unfractionated heparin infusion
Unfractionated heparin is an anticoagulant, and active bleeding contraindicates every anticoagulant. Giving it would worsen the hemorrhage; a filter protects the lungs without thinning the blood.

set1.q: A 50-year-old man developed a single large arteriovenous fistula of the forearm after a penetrating injury. It causes swelling and a bruit over the arm. Which is the management for this acquired fistula?
opts: Surgical removal or size reduction

Correct. Acquired fistulas, whether from trauma or from a procedure, are managed surgically by removing the fistula or decreasing its size. Embolization is an option sometimes used for congenital fistulas.
Compression stockings alone
Elastic support is the conservative approach for congenital fistulas with numerous communications. An acquired single large fistula from trauma is treated surgically.
Warm compresses and elevation
Compresses and elevation are for superficial thrombophlebitis of a vein. They do nothing for an abnormal artery to vein connection, which is managed surgically when acquired.
Lifelong anticoagulation alone
Anticoagulation treats thrombosis and does not close a fistula. The connection from a penetrating injury is repaired by removing it or decreasing its size.

opts: Vascular specialist

Cardiologist
Varicose veins are a superficial venous disease, not a cardiac one. Significant saphenous reflux is referred to a vascular specialist.
Hematologist
A hematologist evaluates clotting disorders, and reflux in a saphenous vein is a valve problem. The appropriate referral is to a vascular specialist.

An orthopedic surgeon treats bone and joint disease. Significant saphenous reflux is referred to a vascular specialist for venous intervention.

set1.q: A 69-year-old man receiving an unfractionated heparin infusion for deep vein thrombosis develops life-threatening bleeding. Which agent reverses the heparin?
opts: Protamine sulfate
Correct. Protamine sulfate is the reversal agent for unfractionated heparin and low molecular weight heparin when bleeding is life-threatening. Each anticoagulant has its own specific reversal agent.
Idarucizumab
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, and does nothing for heparin. The agent that neutralizes heparin is protamine sulfate.
Andexanet alfa
Andexanet alfa reverses the direct factor Xa inhibitors apixaban and rivaroxaban. Heparin is reversed instead by protamine sulfate.
Vitamin K by mouth
Oral vitamin K is a warfarin reversal option and works slowly. Heparin has its own reversal agent, protamine sulfate, which acts on the drug directly.

set1.q: A 74-year-old man with diabetes has a painful ulcer over the lateral ankle. His foot is cool and the pedal pulses are weak. Which test should be obtained next?
opts: Punch biopsy of the ulcer
A biopsy is used when the cause stays uncertain after examination. Weak pulses and a lateral ulcer already suggest arterial disease, so the ankle-brachial index comes first.
Ankle-brachial index

Correct. A painful lateral ankle ulcer with weak pulses suggests arterial insufficiency, and the arterial pulse examination with the ankle-brachial index is performed on any lower extremity wound to look for it.
Venous duplex ultrasound
Duplex assesses venous patency and valve reflux. The lateral location, pain and weak pulses point to an arterial cause, which the ankle-brachial index screens for.
Catheter-based venography
Venography is the invasive venous gold standard, reserved for planning an intervention. It does not evaluate the arterial supply behind this ulcer.

set1.q: A 44-year-old man develops a first calf deep vein thrombosis one week after minor knee arthroscopy under a local nerve block, followed by a long car trip. Which duration of anticoagulation is appropriate?
opts: A fixed three months

Three months is for a major transient risk factor such as surgery under general anesthesia, prolonged hospitalization or major trauma. His minor surgery and travel are minor factors, warranting three to six months.
Indefinitely
Indefinite treatment is reserved for an unprovoked first clot. His clot has identifiable transient triggers, so open-ended anticoagulation is not needed.
Six weeks
Six weeks is below the three-month minimum that applies to every first venous thromboembolism. His clot warrants three to six months.
Three to six months

Correct. A clot provoked by a minor transient risk factor, such as estrogen therapy, pregnancy, minor surgery, prolonged travel or minor leg injury, is treated for three to six months, chosen from the patient's history.

set1.q: A 42-year-old woman has symptomatic varicose veins that did not improve with stockings. She prefers a nonsurgical procedure in which a solution is injected to scar and close the veins. Which procedure fits?
opts: Vein stripping
Stripping is a surgical procedure that removes the vein rather than an injection that closes it. It is a surgical reflux treatment, not the injection she prefers.
Radiofrequency ablation
Radiofrequency uses a catheter to treat reflux with heat, and nothing is injected. The injection of a solution to scar the vein is sclerotherapy.
Venous bypass
Bypass is successful in select patients with chronic venous insufficiency and is a major surgery. It does not close veins, which sclerotherapy does by injection.
Sclerotherapy
Correct. Sclerotherapy is the injection of a sclerosing agent to fibrose and obliterate the veins, one of the interventions for varicose veins along with stripping and catheter-based ablation.

set1.q: A 24-year-old soccer player comes to urgent care with left calf pain that began two days ago when he felt a sudden pull while sprinting, and he has bruising around the ankle. He has no leg swelling, tenderness along the deep veins, cancer, cast or history of clots. By the Wells criteria, a calf muscle tear is at least as likely as deep vein thrombosis. Which is the most appropriate first test?
opts: D-dimer blood test

Correct. The likelier alternative diagnosis subtracts 2 from his Wells score, giving a low likelihood. Low-likelihood patients start with a D-dimer, and a negative result lets the clinician stop, since D-dimer is a sensitive rule-out test.
Venous duplex ultrasound

Venous duplex ultrasound is ordered first for a high Wells score, or after a positive D-dimer. For this low-likelihood patient it is not the first test, because a negative D-dimer could end the work-up.
Contrast ascending venography
Contrast ascending venography is invasive and has been replaced by duplex ultrasound. It is not an initial test for a low-likelihood patient, whose first step is a D-dimer.
Computed tomography of the leg
Computed tomography of the leg is not part of the deep vein thrombosis pathway, which relies on the D-dimer for low-likelihood patients and venous duplex ultrasound for confirmation.

set1.q: A 27-year-old woman has a first deep vein thrombosis of the left leg. Genetic testing shows factor V Leiden, an inherited clotting abnormality. Which component of the Virchow triad does this finding represent?
opts: Venous insufficiency
Venous insufficiency, such as valve failure, is listed under venous stasis rather than clotting tendency. An inherited change in a clotting factor is a hypercoagulable state, the correct component.
Hypercoagulable state

Correct. Factor V Leiden is an inherited hypercoagulable state, like prothrombin gene mutation and protein C, protein S or antithrombin deficiency. It makes the blood clot too readily, the hypercoagulable component of the triad.
Venous stasis

Venous stasis means slowed flow from immobilization, heart failure or venous insufficiency. Her gene change alters the blood's clotting tendency, not its flow, so it belongs in the hypercoagulable component.
Endothelial trauma

Endothelial trauma is injury to the vein wall from surgery, fracture, burns or injection. Factor V Leiden leaves the vessel lining intact and changes coagulation, which is the hypercoagulable component instead.

set1.q: A 66-year-old man has long-standing pitting edema of the lower leg with brown pigmentation and a healed medial ankle ulcer. Duplex ultrasound shows thickened, scarred valve leaflets and chronic obstruction of the femoral vein. He does not recall any leg clot. Which is the most likely cause of his condition?
opts: Congenital arteriovenous fistula
A fistula is a rare cause that produces venous hypertension by shunting arterial blood. Scarred valves and femoral vein obstruction are the signature of a prior clot.
Pelvic vein neoplastic obstruction
A pelvic tumor can obstruct venous outflow, but it does not scar the valve leaflets of the leg veins. Post-thrombotic valve scarring points to an earlier deep vein thrombosis.
Prior deep vein thrombosis

Correct. Scarred valve leaflets with chronic proximal obstruction are post-thrombotic changes, and prior deep vein thrombosis is the leading cause even though about a quarter of patients recall no clot.
Progressive superficial reflux
Superficial reflux is another common cause, but it produces dilated veins with incompetent valves. Thickened, scarred leaflets with obstruction point to an earlier clot.

opts: Recent pregnancy
Women are at higher risk after pregnancy, and it is a recognized risk factor. Family history remains the most common predisposing factor for varicose veins.
Regular heavy lifting
Heavy lifting produces periods of high venous pressure and adds risk. It is less common than family history, the leading predisposing factor for this condition.
Family history of varicose veins
Correct. The most common predisposing factor for varicose veins is family history, so ask whether relatives have them, and how old they were when they developed.
Prolonged standing at work
Long periods of standing raise venous pressure and are a recognized risk factor. It is not the most common predisposing factor, which is family history.

set1.q: A 59-year-old woman had a left leg deep vein thrombosis 11 months ago. She now has chronic left leg heaviness, edema and brownish ankle skin that worsen with standing and improve with elevation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Recurrent deep vein thrombosis
A recurrent clot would usually present acutely with new swelling, pain and warmth. Slowly progressive heaviness with skin change, relieved by elevation, points to chronic venous disease.
Lymphedema

Lymphedema is chronic swelling that usually follows pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation, and brownish hemosiderin staining is rare in it. Her prior leg clot, brown ankle skin and heaviness that eases with elevation point to a venous cause.
Drug-induced edema
Drug-induced edema, such as from dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, is usually bilateral without inflammation. Her unilateral swelling after a leg clot points to post-thrombotic syndrome.
Post-thrombotic syndrome

Correct. Post-thrombotic (postphlebitic) syndrome is symptomatic chronic venous insufficiency that follows a deep vein thrombosis, appearing 6 to 24 months later, with heaviness, edema and brownish skin change from venous hypertension.

set1.q: A 67-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer on active treatment presents to the emergency department with a swollen right leg. The entire leg is swollen and the right calf measures 4 cm more than the left. No alternative diagnosis is judged as likely as deep vein thrombosis, and no other Wells criteria are present. Which is the best next test?
opts: Ankle-brachial index
The ankle-brachial index tests arterial flow to the leg and does not detect venous thrombosis. A high Wells score calls for duplex ultrasound.
Venous duplex ultrasound

Correct. Active cancer, a swollen entire leg and calf swelling over 3 cm give a Wells score of 3, meaning thrombosis is likely. High-probability patients skip the D-dimer and go straight to ultrasound.
D-dimer assay first
A D-dimer is the first test for low or moderate Wells scores, where a negative result rules out clot. At a score of 3 or higher the probability is high, so ultrasound is ordered directly.
Contrast ascending venography
Venography is the historic gold standard but is invasive and has been replaced by venous duplex ultrasound of the involved extremity as the test for deep vein thrombosis.

set1.q: A 62-year-old woman on chemotherapy for breast cancer comes to the emergency department with a calf 4 cm larger than the other, tenderness along the deep veins and no better explanation, so her Wells score is high. Her D-dimer, drawn at triage, is negative. Which action should be avoided?
opts: Ordering a venous duplex ultrasound
Ultrasound is exactly what a high Wells score calls for, whatever the D-dimer shows. It is the appropriate next test, so ordering it is the right action, not one to avoid.
Asking about shortness of breath
Pointed questions about breathing are part of the evaluation, because the lower-extremity clot can send an embolus to the lungs. This is good practice rather than a mistake to avoid.
Measuring both calf circumferences
Comparing the calves at a set point below the tibial tuberosity is how the Wells item for swelling over 3 cm is scored. It is a useful step, not an error.
Ending the work-up at the D-dimer

Correct. With a high Wells score the D-dimer is skipped, or if it was drawn, a negative result does not end the evaluation: she still goes to venous duplex ultrasound. Stopping here risks missing a clot with high pretest probability.

opts: Feeling for a thrill over it
Light palpation for a thrill does not compress the fistula and is safe. Palpation is a core part of the examination that establishes the diagnosis.
Checking pulses below it
Distal pulses should be checked to look for evidence of ischemia. This routine assessment does not compress a large fistula and does not trigger a reflex slowing of the heart.
Holding the fistula compressed
Correct. Compressing a large fistula reflexly slows the heart rate, so sustained manual compression risks a significant fall in pulse and should be avoided during the examination.
Listening over it for a bruit

set1.q: A 71-year-old man hospitalized for six days with pneumonia develops swelling of the left calf. His team considers using the Wells criteria to estimate his probability of deep vein thrombosis. Which statement about applying the Wells criteria to him is accurate?
opts: Meant for outpatient or emergency use

Correct. The Wells criteria are used in the outpatient and emergency department settings, not for inpatients, in whom the score is less useful. A hospitalized patient needs clinical judgment and ultrasound rather than this pathway.
Most accurate in hospitalized patients
The score is less useful in hospitalized patients; it is validated for outpatients and emergency department patients. Inpatients need clinical judgment and ultrasound instead of this pathway.
Designed for upper-extremity clots
The Wells criteria for deep vein thrombosis address suspected leg clots, with items such as calf swelling and pitting edema of the leg. Upper-extremity clots are not what this score was built for.
A low score replaces all testing
A low score does not replace testing; it leads to a D-dimer first, and only a negative result stops the work-up. The score guides which test comes next, not whether to test.

set1.q: A 71-year-old man has been on strict bed rest for six days during an admission for pneumonia and now has swelling and aching of the entire left leg. Which component of the Virchow triad does his prolonged bed rest represent?
opts: Endothelial trauma
Endothelial trauma is direct injury to the vein wall from surgery, fracture, burns, catheters or injection. Bed rest for pneumonia does not injure the vessel lining; it slows flow, which is stasis.
Arterial vasospasm
Arterial vasospasm is not a component of the Virchow triad, which comprises venous stasis, hypercoagulable state and endothelial trauma. Immobility acts on the veins by slowing their blood flow.
Venous stasis

Correct. Bed rest is immobilization, which alters blood flow and lets blood pool in the leg veins, the venous stasis component of the Virchow triad. Prolonged immobilization raises the risk of deep vein thrombosis about twenty-fold.
Hypercoagulable state

A hypercoagulable state is an inherited or acquired clotting tendency, such as factor V Leiden, cancer, estrogen use or pregnancy. Lying still changes blood flow rather than clotting chemistry, so it is stasis.

opts: It rises only with pulmonary embolism
D-dimer rises with fibrinolysis anywhere in the body, including after trauma, and is useful as a rule-out test for both deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. It is not limited to one disease.
It rises only with thigh clots

It reflects fibrinolysis from many causes

Correct. D-dimer elevation implies increased fibrinolysis, but it is sensitive and not specific. Bruising, surgery, cancer and many other conditions raise it, so a positive result needs imaging while a negative one helps rule out a clot.

This reverses the facts: D-dimer is sensitive but not specific. Its sensitivity is why a negative result helps rule out a clot, and its poor specificity is why a positive one needs imaging.

opts: Aspirin alone

Anticoagulation

opts: Acute myocardial infarction

opts: Reexamination in 24 to 48 hours

set1.q: A 64-year-old woman must stay in bed for several days after major abdominal surgery. Her team wants a preventive measure aimed at the venous stasis component of the Virchow triad. Which measure is most appropriate?
opts: Intermittent pneumatic compression

Correct. Intermittent pneumatic compression, sequential devices that squeeze the legs in turn, imitates the calf muscle pump and keeps blood moving, countering stasis. It is used especially when a patient is immobilized after surgery or hospitalized for long.
Inferior vena cava filter

Feel for a vibrating thrill

opts: Oral flavonoid therapy
Flavonoids are used to increase venous tone and do not treat infection. Warmth, tenderness and fever describe cellulitis, which requires an oral antibiotic.
Oral cephalexin
Correct. Cellulitis complicating venous insufficiency is treated with oral antibiotics, and cephalexin or clindamycin is recommended. Topical therapy is not adequate for the infection.

set2.q: A 49-year-old man has a first proximal deep vein thrombosis with no surgery, trauma, hormone use, travel, cancer or other identifiable trigger, and no inherited disorder has been found. How long should anticoagulation continue?
opts: Three to six months
Three to six months fits a clot provoked by a minor transient factor such as estrogen therapy, pregnancy, minor surgery or travel. An unprovoked clot has no such trigger and needs longer therapy.
Six weeks
Six weeks is shorter than the minimum of three months required after any first venous thromboembolism. An unprovoked clot needs indefinite therapy.
Indefinitely

Correct. A first venous thromboembolism with no identifiable risk factor is unprovoked, and its source, such as an undiscovered inherited clotting disorder, is unknown. Treatment therefore continues for an indefinite length of time.
Three months
Three months is the minimum for a clot provoked by a major transient risk factor such as surgery or major trauma. An unprovoked clot has no reversible trigger, so treatment continues beyond it.

set2.q: A 74-year-old woman has chronic leg swelling, brown discoloration from hemosiderin and a shallow ulcer above the medial ankle. Her pedal pulses are weak and her ankle-brachial index is 0.6 on that leg. Which treatment should be avoided until her arterial disease is addressed?
opts: Skin emollients
Emollients maintain the skin barrier, prevent dryness and fissuring, and reduce scratching in venous stasis changes. They involve no pressure on the limb and are not held back for arterial disease.
Graduated compression

Correct. Compression is standard treatment for venous insufficiency but is contraindicated in peripheral artery disease, so the ankle-brachial index must be checked first. An index of 0.9 or less indicates disease.
Gentle skin cleansing
Cleansing removes dirt and keeps the skin barrier healthy in venous stasis changes. It applies no pressure to the limb, so it is not held back for arterial disease, unlike compression.
Daily walking with ankle flexion
Exercise strengthens the calf muscle pump and is recommended for venous disease. It does not compress the limb, so it does not carry the arterial risk of compression.

set2.q: A 62-year-old man on hemodialysis has a left forearm arteriovenous fistula that was created four months ago. Last month it had a palpable thrill (a vibration felt over the access) and a soft bruit. At today's visit no thrill can be felt and no bruit is heard over the access. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Repeat examination in 7 to 10 days
The 7 to 10 day recheck belongs to superficial thrombophlebitis. Dialysis access that has lost its thrill and bruit should not wait, because the fistula is no longer functioning.
Urgent referral for access evaluation

Correct. A healthy fistula has a diffuse thrill and a soft bruit with systolic and diastolic components. Loss of both means the access is no longer working, so it needs prompt referral to the specialist.
Reassurance with routine follow-up
Reassurance would miss a failing access. A working fistula carries a thrill and a soft bruit, so absence of both is abnormal and warrants prompt specialist evaluation.
Warm compresses and an anti-inflammatory drug
That regimen treats superficial thrombophlebitis of a vein. A fistula without thrill or bruit has a flow problem that needs specialist evaluation, not symptomatic care.

opts: Intensive care unit monitoring
Intensive monitoring is not required for a stable patient with an uncomplicated calf clot and low bleeding risk. Outpatient anticoagulation is appropriate for him.
Observation without treatment
Anticoagulation is the mainstay of treatment and is needed for at least three months. Withholding it would leave the clot free to propagate or embolize.
Outpatient anticoagulation
Correct. Outpatient therapy suits patients who are hemodynamically stable, have low bleeding risk and no renal insufficiency, and have good support with reliable follow-up. He meets every criterion.
Hospital admission for heparin
Admission is for iliofemoral clots, symptomatic pulmonary embolism, high bleeding risk or comorbidities needing inpatient care. He has none of these, so he can be treated at home.

set2.q: A 58-year-old man with large varicose veins in the right leg has a painful, red, indurated cord along the medial calf that developed over two days. He is afebrile and has no swelling of the leg. Which study confirms the diagnosis and is considered the gold standard?
opts: Venous duplex ultrasound

Correct. Venous duplex ultrasound is the gold standard, showing a noncompressible superficial vein with clot and thickening of the vein wall. History and examination suggest the diagnosis, and the ultrasound confirms it.
D-dimer assay
D-dimer rises whenever fibrinolysis occurs anywhere, so it is sensitive but not specific and cannot confirm a superficial clot. Confirmation of superficial thrombophlebitis is by duplex ultrasound.
Contrast ascending venography
Contrast venography was the historic gold standard for deep vein thrombosis and has been replaced by duplex ultrasound. It is invasive and is not used to confirm a superficial vein clot.
Ankle-brachial index
The ankle-brachial index measures arterial inflow and screens for peripheral artery disease. It does not image the vein, so it cannot show a noncompressible superficial vein containing clot.

set2.q: A 61-year-old woman with prior deep vein thrombosis has leg edema and brown pigmentation. Duplex ultrasound is performed to explain her symptoms. Which finding is expected?
opts: Noncompressible calcified arteries

Noncompressible calcified arteries are an artery-wall problem that can falsely raise the ankle-brachial index; they are not what venous duplex looks for. In venous insufficiency the ultrasound shows incompetent valves with reflux.
Narrowed superficial femoral artery
Arterial stenosis causes claudication and is not the target of venous duplex. The expected finding here is valvular incompetence with reflux.
Dilated lymphatic channels
Lymphatic channels are not the target of venous duplex, and lymphedema is a differential diagnosis. In insufficiency the ultrasound shows valve reflux.
Incompetent venous valves with reflux

Correct. Duplex ultrasound assesses venous patency and valve competence, and chronic venous insufficiency shows valves that fail to stop blood flowing back toward the foot, producing venous hypertension.

set2.q: A 44-year-old man has a large arteriovenous fistula of the thigh that was diagnosed on physical examination. Before repair, the vascular surgeon needs the exact location and size of the connection. Which study provides this information?
opts: Punch biopsy of the skin
A punch biopsy is used to work up skin lesions such as ulcers of uncertain cause. It provides no information on the vessels or the size of a fistula.
Computed tomography angiography
Correct. Computed tomography angiography and conventional angiography can confirm an arteriovenous fistula and give information about its location and size, helping to plan repair.
Ankle-brachial index
The ankle-brachial index measures pressure at the ankle relative to the arm to screen for arterial disease. It cannot show where an arteriovenous connection lies or how large it is.
Plain radiograph of the thigh
A plain radiograph outlines bone and calcification but not blood vessels. Location and size of a fistula come from angiographic imaging, not from a plain film.

set2.q: A 47-year-old woman has a tender, red, firm segment along a forearm vein after a peripheral intravenous catheter was removed. Venous duplex ultrasound shows a superficial vein with a thickened wall. Which additional finding would establish thrombophlebitis rather than phlebitis alone?
opts: Clot within the vein lumen

Correct. Wall thickening alone is phlebitis, inflammation of the vein wall without thrombus. Thickening together with clot in the lumen is thrombophlebitis, and the distinction matters because treatment differs.
Thickening of the vein wall
Wall thickening is already present and is common to both phlebitis and thrombophlebitis. Only clot within the lumen turns the picture into thrombophlebitis.
Reflux through incompetent valves
Valve reflux belongs to chronic venous disease such as varicose veins and chronic venous insufficiency. It says nothing about clot inside an inflamed superficial vein.
Fluid collection around the vein
A perivenous fluid collection would raise concern for abscess or infection around the vein. Thrombophlebitis is defined by clot within the lumen of the thickened vein.

set2.q: A 70-year-old woman with heart failure is admitted with a tender, swollen left calf, and duplex ultrasound confirms deep vein thrombosis. Her daughter asks why heart failure raises the risk of a clot. Which Virchow triad component should the clinician name?
opts: Elevated platelet count
An elevated platelet count is not one of the three Virchow triad components. Heart failure raises clotting risk through slowed venous flow, which is venous stasis.
Venous stasis
Correct. Heart failure is listed under venous stasis, the Virchow component reflecting altered blood flow. A weak pump lets blood pool and slow in the veins of the legs, so clots form more readily.
Hypercoagulable state

A hypercoagulable state comes from inherited thrombophilia, cancer, estrogen therapy or pregnancy. Heart failure raises clot risk by slowing venous return, which is stasis rather than a change in clotting chemistry.
Endothelial trauma
Endothelial trauma is injury to the vein wall from surgery, fracture, burns or injection. Heart failure does not damage the vessel lining; it reduces venous flow, the stasis component.

set2.q: A 74-year-old woman with newly diagnosed deep vein thrombosis has chronic kidney disease with a creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min. Which approach should be avoided?
opts: Overlapping heparin with warfarin
Heparin is given together with warfarin for at least five days and until the international normalized ratio is above 2 for at least 24 hours. This overlap is standard, not a mistake.
Beginning therapy as an outpatient

Correct. Patients with a creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min are hospitalized to start treatment, because renal insufficiency also excludes outpatient therapy. Starting at home is the approach to avoid.
Admission for intravenous heparin

Hospital admission for unfractionated heparin, given as a loading bolus then a continuous infusion, is the recommended approach for severe renal disease, so it is appropriate rather than one to avoid.
Adjusting heparin by lab results
Unfractionated heparin is titrated to the activated partial thromboplastin time, so laboratory-guided adjustment is standard and appropriate rather than an error.

opts: Dabigatran

Dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor, is started only after about five days of parenteral therapy. It does not follow the loading-then-maintenance oral monotherapy strategy that this plan describes.
Edoxaban
Edoxaban is an anti-Xa agent, but it also follows five days of parenteral anticoagulation rather than serving as a stand-alone oral loading strategy. Apixaban fits an oral-only plan.
Fondaparinux
Fondaparinux is an indirect factor Xa inhibitor given by injection, so it cannot be the oral monotherapy the plan describes. Apixaban is the oral direct factor Xa inhibitor for that strategy.

Correct. Apixaban, a direct factor Xa inhibitor, is given as oral monotherapy with a loading dose followed by a maintenance dose, one of the three major anticoagulation strategies. Rivaroxaban follows the same pattern.

opts: D-dimer assay
D-dimer only signals fibrinolysis somewhere in the body and shows no vascular anatomy. Confirming an abnormal artery to vein connection at the groin requires duplex ultrasound.
Ankle-brachial index
The ankle-brachial index compares ankle and arm pressures to screen for peripheral artery disease. It does not image the groin or demonstrate an abnormal connection between artery and vein.

A plain radiograph shows bone and calcification but not blood flow. Duplex ultrasound displays flow and confirms a suspected fistula at the femoral puncture site.

opts: Venous duplex ultrasound

Correct. Venous duplex ultrasound of the involved extremity is the diagnostic test for deep vein thrombosis, including arm clots from central venous catheters. It has replaced venography, the old invasive gold standard.
Contrast ascending venography
Contrast ascending venography was the gold standard but is invasive and has been replaced by venous duplex ultrasound. It is not the first test for a catheter-related arm clot.
Ankle-brachial index
The ankle-brachial index compares ankle and arm pressures to detect peripheral artery disease in the legs. It does not evaluate a swollen arm for a venous clot.

set2.q: A 60-year-old man has had untreated varicose veins for many years. He now has persistent lower leg swelling, brown skin discoloration and a shallow ulcer above the medial ankle. Untreated long-standing varicose veins can progress to which condition?
opts: Lymphedema
Lymphedema arises from lymphatic obstruction and is not a progression of varicose veins. Venous hypertension leads to insufficiency with brown pigmentation and ulcers.
Arteriovenous fistula
A fistula is an abnormal artery-to-vein connection, acquired or created, and does not develop from varicose veins. Long-standing reflux progresses to venous insufficiency.
Chronic venous insufficiency
Correct. Long-standing varicose veins can progress to chronic venous insufficiency, with edema, skin changes and venous ulceration from sustained venous hypertension.

set2.q: A 32-year-old woman who is 34 weeks pregnant sits in a car for nine hours and develops left calf swelling and pain. Her pregnancy supplies a hypercoagulable state and the long ride supplies venous stasis. Which additional component would complete the Virchow triad?
opts: Endothelial trauma

Correct. The Virchow triad is venous stasis, hypercoagulable state and endothelial trauma. Pregnancy and the car ride supply two components, so the missing one is injury to the vein wall, as from trauma, surgery, burns or injection.
Venous stasis
Venous stasis is already present from nine hours of sitting still, so it cannot be the additional component. The one still missing is endothelial trauma, injury to the vessel wall.
Hypercoagulable state
Pregnancy already supplies the hypercoagulable state by raising clotting tendency, so it is present rather than missing. The component still absent is endothelial trauma.
Arterial thrombosis
Arterial thrombosis is a clot in an artery and is not a component of the Virchow triad. The venous component still absent in this scenario is endothelial trauma.

set2.q: A 44-year-old man seen in an outpatient clinic has had left calf pain and swelling for three days. A plaster cast was removed from his left leg yesterday after four weeks for a tibial fracture. Examination shows pitting edema confined to the left leg. He meets no other Wells criteria, and no alternative diagnosis is judged as likely as deep vein thrombosis. Which is the most appropriate next test?
opts: D-dimer assay

Correct. Recent plaster immobilization and pitting edema in the symptomatic leg give a Wells score of 2, a moderate pretest probability. Patients scoring 1 to 2 need a D-dimer, and a negative result rules out the diagnosis.
Venous duplex ultrasound
Ultrasound is ordered first when the Wells score is 3 or higher and thrombosis is likely. At a score of 2 the D-dimer comes first, and ultrasound follows only if it is positive.
Contrast ascending venography
Venography is invasive and has been replaced by duplex ultrasound for confirming deep vein thrombosis. It is not the next test at a moderate Wells score.

set2.q: A 36-year-old woman who smokes and takes an oral contraceptive has mild calf aching. Her Wells score is low, and her D-dimer returns positive. What is the next step?
opts: Venous duplex ultrasound

Correct. In a low-likelihood patient a positive D-dimer cannot exclude deep vein thrombosis, so venous duplex ultrasound follows. A positive ultrasound makes the diagnosis; a negative one rules it out.
Empiric anticoagulation alone
Treating without imaging exposes her to bleeding risk on an unconfirmed diagnosis, and a positive D-dimer is nonspecific. Ultrasound confirms or excludes the clot before anticoagulation is committed.
Reassurance and discharge
Discharge is for a negative D-dimer in a low-likelihood patient. A positive result means fibrinolysis is occurring somewhere and needs ultrasound to find out whether it is a clot.

set2.q: A 76-year-old man has had symmetric pitting swelling of both ankles for three weeks. He started amlodipine for hypertension one month ago. There is no warmth, redness, tenderness or skin discoloration, and he has no history of heart, kidney or liver disease. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Chronic venous insufficiency
Chronic venous insufficiency produces brownish pigmentation, dermatitis and eventually ulceration after years of venous hypertension. Three weeks of bland swelling after a new drug does not fit.
Lymphedema
Lymphedema is chronic swelling, usually unilateral, often after pelvic surgery, malignancy or radiation. This bilateral swelling began soon after starting a calcium channel blocker.
Drug-induced edema
Correct. Swelling that is often bilateral, without signs of inflammation, is a common adverse effect of some drugs, including dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine.
Bilateral deep vein thrombosis
Deep vein thrombosis is usually unilateral and brings pain, warmth and erythema. Symmetric painless swelling that began after a new drug without inflammation fits medication-induced edema.

set2.q: A 57-year-old man with knee osteoarthritis felt a sudden sharp pain behind the right knee while climbing stairs, followed by severe calf discomfort and swelling. Venous duplex ultrasound shows no thrombus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Superficial thrombophlebitis
Superficial thrombophlebitis gives a tender, indurated cord along a superficial vein with local redness. A sudden severe calf pain that began behind the knee is not a superficial vein process.
Ruptured popliteal (Baker) cyst

Correct. A ruptured popliteal (Baker) cyst produces severe, sudden calf discomfort that mimics deep vein thrombosis, and the ultrasound shows no clot. It is a standard item on the differential of a swollen calf.
Calf muscle tear
A calf muscle tear follows an inciting injury and may leave bruising at the ankle. Here the pain began behind the knee during ordinary activity, which fits a ruptured cyst better.
Post-thrombotic syndrome
Post-thrombotic syndrome is chronic venous insufficiency appearing 6 to 24 months after a clot, with slow-onset edema and skin change. A sudden calf event with no prior clot is not that.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man taking apixaban for deep vein thrombosis develops an acute intracranial hemorrhage. Which agent reverses the anticoagulant?
opts: Andexanet alfa

Correct. Andexanet alfa reverses the direct factor Xa inhibitors apixaban and rivaroxaban in life-threatening or intracranial bleeding, and it is also used off-label for edoxaban. Hemorrhage is the most serious adverse effect of anticoagulation.
Protamine sulfate
Protamine sulfate reverses unfractionated heparin and low molecular weight heparin. Apixaban is a direct factor Xa inhibitor, and its reversal agent is andexanet alfa.
Idarucizumab
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor. Apixaban is an anti-Xa agent, so its reversal agent is andexanet alfa.
Vitamin K by mouth
Oral vitamin K corrects warfarin, not the direct factor Xa inhibitors. For apixaban with intracranial bleeding, the specific reversal agent is andexanet alfa.
